Traceroute Analyzer

Run traceroute on your own computer, paste the result here, and get a hop-by-hop table with latency, loss and an explanation of what is normal and what is a real problem.

1. Run a trace on your computer

SystemCommand
Windowstracert -d example.org
Linuxtraceroute -n example.org
macOStraceroute -n example.org
MTR (report mode)mtr -rwn -c 20 example.org
Cisco IOStraceroute example.org

2. Paste the output

What traceroute shows

Traceroute sends probe packets with a gradually increasing time-to-live (TTL). Each router that decrements the TTL to zero returns an ICMP "time exceeded" message, which reveals its address and how long the reply took. The result is a list of the routers between you and the destination, in order, with roughly three timings for each hop.

Browsers cannot generate these probes, so this page works the other way round. You run the command on your own computer, which also tests your own network path, and paste the result here to have it interpreted.

How to read the output

  • Each line is a router. The three times are separate probes to that hop.
  • * * * and "Request timed out" mean no reply came back for that hop within the timeout.
  • Latency is cumulative. Each hop's time is the round trip from you to that router, not the time spent on one link.
  • Hop numbers are not links. Traffic may take a different path on the way back.

Things that look wrong but are not

  • A single hop with * * *. Many routers deprioritise or block probe replies while still forwarding traffic normally. If later hops reply, ignore it.
  • High latency at one middle hop that falls again afterwards. The router is slow to generate a reply, but forwards packets quickly. Only latency that stays high matters.
  • Loss at one hop in an MTR report. If the next hops show no loss, the first router is rate limiting replies. Real loss shows at that hop and every hop after it.
  • Different addresses on the same hop. The path is load-balanced over several links.

Signs of a real problem

  • Loss that begins at a hop and continues to the destination.
  • A latency increase that stays at every later hop, and is bigger than the distance would explain.
  • A path that leaves your region and returns, which shows up as unexpectedly high latency to a nearby server.
  • A trace that stops at one router and never reaches the destination, while other destinations work.

When you contact your ISP or hosting provider, send the complete traceroute or MTR report from your side along with the time it was taken. Use the BGP and ASN lookup to find out which network owns an address in the path.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between traceroute, tracert and MTR?

Traceroute is the Linux and macOS command and tracert is the Windows equivalent. MTR combines traceroute and ping, sending many probes over time, so it shows loss and variation per hop more reliably than a single run.

Why does the -n or -d option help?

It skips reverse DNS lookups for each hop, so the trace runs much faster and avoids long pauses.

Why does my trace stop before the destination?

Many firewalls drop probe packets or the ICMP replies, so the last hops show nothing even though the destination works. Try the test with a TCP-based probe such as traceroute -T -p 443 on Linux.

Is the pasted output uploaded?

No. It is analyzed in your browser and never leaves your device.
